title: Chapter 47: Oren's Barrier, Again, Part 1 of 5: Snow on Velvet Street
html:
The real snow came at the half bell after three.
Oren had thought he knew snow. It had been snowing on and off since Monday, when he came into the city under Abner Cole's coal. Thin snow, mostly. Sleety and gray, the kind that comes down sideways and lies for an hour and turns to brown slush in the gutters. He had walked in it every day. He had stopped noticing it.
This was not that.
This came down out of a sky that had gone the color of a bruise, yellow-gray and low, so low that it seemed to rest on the chimneys. It came straight down. No wind at all. Big soft flakes, as big as the end of his thumb, so many and so close together that the far end of the street was gone, and then the middle of the street, and then the houses on the other side, until he and the girl were walking in a small gray room made of falling white, with no walls, and no roof, and the sound of the city gone small and far away, as if somebody had put a blanket over it.
It lay on his shoulders. It lay on the brim of his hat. It lay on the girl's cap in front of him, and on her shoulders, so that she looked like a figure in a sugar shop window.
He walked one pace behind her, and one pace to her left. The way he had always walked behind her, since she was nine years old and her father had first said, Captain, take Lyra to the park. One pace behind and one to the left, so that his sword arm was free and his body was between her and the street.
His sword was under Terrence's coat. Along his left leg, in its scabbard, with the hilt up under his arm where the coat hid it. It made him walk a little stiffly. He did not mind. He had walked stiffly with a sword under his coat for thirty years.
And he read.
He had not noticed he was doing it, at first. Not for the first few streets, coming down Saint Bride's Hill in the snow. Then he noticed, and could not stop. He was reading everything. Every sign. Every board over every shop. Every notice pasted on every wall, and every name on every brass plate beside every door. He read them the way a starving man reads a menu in a window. Slowly. Every letter.
CHANDLER. CANDLES. ROPE. LAMP OIL.
J. PRIDDY. BOOTS MENDED WHILE YOU WAIT.
COMMIT NO NUISANCE.
He did not know why. He only knew that there was something in him, this afternoon, under the snow and the cold and the weight of the sword, that was hungry for it. For the letters. For the shapes of them. The round ones and the straight ones and the ones with tails. O and I and G. The way they sat next to each other on a board, in a row, and turned into a word, and the word turned into a thing. BOOTS. There. A pair of boots, in his head, out of four marks of paint on a piece of wood.
It was a kind of magic, he thought. He had never thought of it like that before. He had learned his letters at six, in a dame school in a village in the north, from an old woman with a stick who rapped your knuckles if you said them wrong. He had hated it. He had been a slow reader all his life. He read orders, and lists, and the names on doors. He had never read a book through. He did not like them.
But it was a kind of magic. Marks on a board. And a thing in your head.
WANTED for questioning in the matter of the THORNE ABDUCTION.
He read that one too, on the corner of Chandler Row, half covered with snow. He read it to the end. A man aged about thirty, dark, with gray marks upon the hands. Then he read the one beside it, the new one, with the paste still wet under the snow. A GENTLEMAN from the Office will be IN PERSON at the FISH STAIRS on FRIDAY at the EIGHTH BELL. All children of the parish are to attend. Sweets will be given.
Tomorrow, he thought.
He walked on.
They did not go by Comb Street this time. They went the other way. Round the bottom of the Hill, by the old Corn Exchange, and up through the narrow lanes behind Silk Street, where the tailors and the hatters and the glovers had their workshops at the backs of their shops, and the snow lay thick and unbroken on every step. Nobody had been out. Nobody was out now. The lanes were empty. Once a door opened, and a woman looked out, and saw them, and shut it again.
No boy in a gray cap. Oren looked. He looked in every window and every doorway and every dark mouth of every alley. He looked behind them at every corner. The snow made it hard. The snow made it easy, too. A boy following them would leave tracks, and there were no tracks behind them but their own, filling up already, going soft at the edges.
At the top of the last lane, the girl stopped.
She stood with her back to a wall, under the overhang of a roof, out of the falling snow, and turned and looked up at him. Her face was red with cold. There was snow on her eyelashes. She had been very quiet since the tower. She had not said a word, coming down the hill. He had not asked her anything.
"Oren," she said.
"Lady."
"He answered." She said it very low. "Ro. He tapped once. On my hand."
Oren did not say anything. He looked at her for a long moment, under the overhang, with the snow coming down between them like a curtain.
Then he nodded. Once.
She looked at him as if she was waiting for something more. He did not have anything more. He was not good at words. He had never been good at them, even before he started losing them. He stood there in the snow in a dead man's coat—in a live man's coat, Terrence was alive, he had to remember that—in another man's coat, too short in the arms, with his sword along his leg, and nodded.
It seemed to be enough. She turned and went on.
The lane came out at the top into the mews behind Velvet Street. A long cobbled yard, white now from wall to wall, with the backs of the tall houses rising up on one side, and coach houses and stables on the other, their doors shut, and the smell of horses and straw coming faintly through the cold. At the far end of the mews, a high wall with broken glass set along the top of it in a line of green and brown teeth, each one wearing a little cap of snow.
And halfway along, on the house side, the green door, with the brass knocker shaped like a thimble.
The step in front of it had been swept. Recently. Since the snow began. There was a clean dark oblong of stone in front of the door, and only a thin white skin on it, where the newest snow had come down.
Oren looked at that for a moment.
Then he looked up. At the back of the house. Four floors, and a row of attic windows under the roof, little ones, with snow on their sills. On the second floor, a window with a lamp in it already, though it was barely four o'clock. On the roof, the chimneys, smoking. And between two of the chimneys, flat in the slope of the slates, a square of glass. A skylight. With the snow sliding off it, because the glass was warm from the room below.
He noted it. The way he had noted every door and window and stair of every house he had ever walked into behind a Thorne, for twenty-two years. Without thinking. Where the ways out were.
Then he went up to the green door, past the girl, and knocked. Three times, and then once.
And while he waited, he looked up at the painted board over the door. The sign. It was the same as the one at the front, on Velvet Street, he supposed, but smaller and plainer, for tradesmen and deliveries. A narrow board of black, with letters on it in gold. The gold was old and a little rubbed, but you could read it.
THE NEEDLE AND THIMBLE.
And under it, smaller:
MME. HESPER.
He read it twice. He did not know why. He liked the shape of the H. Like a little gate.
The Needle and Thimble
The green door opened on the second knock, before he had finished the third.
Madame Hesper stood in it. Tall and thin, in her black dress buttoned to the chin and her brown apron, with her iron-gray hair pulled back tight and the two long pins through the knot in a cross. Four pins in the corner of her mouth. Spectacles on their silver chain. She looked at the girl. Then she looked past the girl, up, at him, and her long face did not move.
"Captain Oren," she said, round the pins.
"Madame."
"You've been standing on my step for half a minute looking at my sign."
"Yes, Madame."
"Is there something wrong with it?"
Oren thought about it.
"No, Madame," he said. "I liked it."
Madame Hesper looked at him over her spectacles for a moment longer. Then she took the pins out of her mouth, one by one, and pushed them into the cushion on her wrist, and stood back from the door.
"In," she said. "Both of you. You're letting the snow into my passage. Mind the step, it's been swept."
"I saw."
"Bridie did it. Twice. Since noon." She shut the green door behind them and turned the key in it and shot the bolt, top and bottom, the way she had on Wednesday, he supposed, and on Saturday, and every time. "She says she'll do it again at five, if she's passing. She says a swept step is a clean step, and a clean step shows the prints of anyone who comes to it." She looked at Oren. "Bridie Kane is a cleverer woman than half the Archon's Council."
They went along the narrow passage, past a door to a scullery and a door to a coal store, into the back room.
Oren had been in it yesterday. He looked at it again now, the way he always looked at a room the second time, to see what had changed. The long table with its white sheet and its bolts of cloth. The iron stove in the corner, red, with the kettle on it. The cheval glass on its stand. The three dressmaker's dummies in their half-made gowns, standing about in the shadows like guests who had come too early. The smell of starch and warm iron and lavender. Nothing had changed. Except that on the end of the long table, where the box had been yesterday, there was a gown.
Gray silk. Laid out flat on a clean sheet, with its long sleeves folded across its breast like the arms of somebody asleep. It caught the light from the stove and the lamp, and the light moved on it, slowly, the way light moves on water. It was very plain. It had nothing on it at all. No lace. No beads. Only the silk, and the shape of it, and a line of tiny gray buttons down the back, so small and so many that he could not count them.
The girl stopped by the table and looked at it.
She did not touch it. Her red rough hands stayed at her sides. And Oren, behind her, saw her back go very straight and very still, the way it went straight at the end of the barge when she looked north up the river toward the city.
He knew that gown.
He had seen it on the stairs at Crown Walk. A long time ago. A woman coming down slowly, one gloved hand on the rail, and the gray silk moving round her like smoke, and her face turned up to the man at the bottom of the stairs who was waiting for her with his hat in his hand. And Oren, by the front door, in his captain's coat, standing very straight, looking at nothing. The way a guard looks at nothing. Seeing everything.
He did not have many memories of the Lady Isolde. She had not been a woman who talked to the household guard. But he had that one. He had always had it.
He looked away from the gown.
"Dilly," said Madame Hesper. "The kettle."
There was a girl in the room. Oren had not seen her at first. She had been standing in the shadow by the cheval glass, very still, with her hands folded in front of her apron, the way a servant stands who has been told to stand still and not be noticed. She came out of the shadow now, quickly, and went to the stove. She was fifteen, perhaps. Small and thin, with a pointed freckled face and pale red hair scraped back under a white cap, and big frightened eyes. She lifted the kettle off the hob with a cloth round the handle. Her hands were shaking. The kettle lid rattled.
"Dilly is my girl," said Madame Hesper. "For two years now. She does the seams and the hems and the shop when I'm in the back. She has very good small fingers and a mother with a cough." Madame Hesper did not look at her. "She has not been well herself today. She has been dropping things."
"I'm sorry, Madame," said Dilly, very low, at the stove.
"I know you are, child." Madame Hesper turned to the girl in the cap. "Now. Lady Lyra. Coat. Cap. Boots. Everything. Behind the screen. Dilly will hold it." She turned to Oren. "And you, Captain, will go and sit in the shop, out of the way of my pins, and not look round. There's a chair by the counter. Sit in it."
Oren looked at her.
"I'd rather stay by the door, Madame."
"Which door?"
"This one." He looked at the green door at the end of the passage behind him. Bolted top and bottom. "Or that one." At the other door, on the far side of the back room, the one that went through into the shop.
"You can't stay by both."
"No, Madame."
Madame Hesper looked at him for a long moment. Something moved in her long face. Not a smile. Something drier than a smile.
"Then go and sit in the shop," she said, "by the front door. Which is the one that faces the street, and the gas lamps, and the Watch, and the whole of the Hill going by. And I will see to this one." She took two pins from the cushion on her wrist and put them in her mouth. "I have been seeing to my own back door for forty-one years, Captain. I can see to it for an hour more."
Oren went into the shop.
It was a long narrow room, the front of the house, with the street door at one end and the door to the back room at the other. It was colder than the back room. There was no stove. There was a counter of dark polished wood along one side, with a brass rail and a brass measuring rule let into the top of it, and drawers behind it from floor to ceiling, small square drawers, dozens of them, each with a little brass handle and a little white card in a brass frame. He read the cards. He could not help it. BUTTONS, JET. BUTTONS, PEARL. HOOKS & EYES. TAPE, LINEN, 1/2 IN. RIBBON, SATIN, BLACK. There were bolts of cloth on shelves along the other wall, in every color. There was a long glass case with gloves in it, laid out in pairs like hands praying. There was a wooden chair by the counter, with a cushion on it.
And at the end, the window.
It was big. Most of the width of the shop. Small square panes of old glass in a frame of black wood, and in the middle of the window, painted on the glass itself in curving letters of gold, so that you could read them from the street, the name of the shop. From inside, Oren saw them backward. Gold letters, wrong way round, standing in the window between him and the falling snow.
REPSEH .EMM
And above, bigger, in an arch:
ELBMIHT DNA ELDEEN EHT
He stood and looked at them for a while. It took him a moment to read them backward. He did it slowly, letter by letter, from the right. T. H. E. The. N. E. E. D. L. E. Needle. It was like reading something in a mirror. It made his head feel strange.
Beyond the gold letters, Velvet Street was white.
It was a fine wide street, on the shoulder of the Hill, with tall cream-colored houses all along it and shop fronts at the bottom of them with bow windows and painted signs. Gas lamps on iron posts, already lit, though it was barely four, each with a little cap of snow on top and a soft yellow ball of light round it in the falling white. The snow had covered everything. The pavements. The road. The steps. The railings. A carriage went by, slowly, with its lamps lit, the horses' hooves making no sound at all in the snow, only the creak of the harness and the soft hiss of the wheels.
Then nothing. The street was empty.
Oren did not sit in the chair.
He moved it. He picked it up and set it down again in the corner by the window, where the wall met the glass, with its back to the wall, so that he could see the street through the window, and the street door beside him, and the door to the back room at the far end of the shop, all at once, without turning his head.
Then he sat down on it, with his sword along his leg under Terrence's coat, and his hand on his knee near the hilt.
And waited.
Behind him, through the door to the back room, he could hear them. The rustle of cloth. Madame Hesper's voice, low and sharp, round the pins. Arms up. Turn. Turn back. Hold still, child, I said hold the screen still, not shake it like a sheet on a line. And the girl's voice, saying nothing. And the kettle beginning, very softly, to sing.
